note: Interpretive content for the attachment analysis, keyed by the pattern labels in ecrr_mapping.json combined_patterns.

sources.accuracy: Mario Mikulincer & Phillip R. Shaver, Attachment in Adulthood (2nd ed., Guilford, 2016): the two-dimension model (anxiety and avoidance as continuous scores), the idea of hyperactivating (anxious) and deactivating (avoidant) strategies, and evidence that attachment can change through secure relationships and practice.
sources.practical_tips: Amir Levine & Rachel Heller, Attached (2010): practical relationship tips (e.g. effective communication of needs). Its fixed-type framing and its harsher treatment of avoidance are deliberately not used.
sources.status: Drafted from these works' widely published concepts, without the books at hand. Check wording against the books before launch.

Secure.in_practice: You can let people close without losing yourself, and you can be apart without assuming the worst. Conflict tends to feel repairable rather than threatening.
growth: Keep doing what works: saying what you need directly and trusting the answer.
Your steadiness can help a less secure partner feel safe; patience with their worry or distance goes a long way.
Security isn't fixed: long stress or a painful loss can shake it, and that is normal.

Anxious-preoccupied.in_practice: Closeness matters deeply to you, and when a partner seems distant your mind fills the gap with worry. You may seek reassurance, or read small signs as big ones.
growth: Notice the moment worry starts telling a story, and check the facts with your partner before acting on it.
Ask for reassurance directly instead of testing for it.
Build steadiness outside the relationship too: friends, practice, routine and time that is just yours.

Dismissive-avoidant.in_practice: You value independence and handle things yourself. When someone wants more closeness than feels comfortable, you may pull back, go quiet or get busy.
growth: Notice when you pull away as closeness grows, and name it rather than disappear.
Try sharing one small thing you would normally keep to yourself.
Letting someone help is a skill, not a weakness; independence and closeness can grow together.

Fearful-avoidant.in_practice: You want closeness and brace against it at the same time. Relationships can swing between reaching out and protecting yourself, which is tiring from the inside.
growth: Both the wish for closeness and the caution make sense; notice which one is active in the moment.
Go slowly: small, consistent experiences of safety do more than big leaps.
This pattern often softens with a therapist's support, and it is worth considering.

dimension_notes.ANX_high: When closeness feels uncertain, your attachment system turns up the volume: you watch for signs of distance, seek contact, and find it hard to settle until you feel reassured. Researchers call these hyperactivating strategies. They are an understandable way of trying to keep someone close, not a flaw.
dimension_notes.AVD_high: When closeness or dependence starts to feel too much, your attachment system turns the volume down: you rely on yourself, keep feelings private and create some distance. Researchers call these deactivating strategies. They often began as a sensible way of coping when leaning on others didn't feel safe.
dimension_notes.both_low: Neither strategy dominates for you: you can reach for closeness when you need it and give space when others need it, without much alarm either way.

can_change: Attachment isn't fixed. Scores move with new relationships, life events and deliberate practice, and people who start out insecure often become more secure over time (researchers call this earned security). Your baseline and retakes will show your own direction.
near_boundary: Your scores sit close to the line between patterns, so the neighbouring pattern ({runner_up}) may describe parts of your experience too.
